sections.h2: What does the North Carolina homestead exclusion do?
sections.html:
It removes part of a qualifying owner's home value from property tax. For the elderly or disabled exclusion, the amount removed is the larger of $25,000 or 50% of the appraised value of the permanent residence.

North Carolina has three separate relief programs aimed at homeowners, and the exclusion is the best known. The state ties them together on a single application, Form AV-9, which you file with your county tax assessor and not with the Department of Revenue. An owner can draw benefit from only one of the three at a time.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the elderly or disabled exclusion in North Carolina?
sections.html:
You qualify if, on January 1 before the tax year, you are a North Carolina resident who is at least 65 or totally and permanently disabled, and your income for the prior year did not pass the eligibility limit. The statute is G.S. 105-277.1.

  • The income limit printed on the 2026 NCDOR form is $38,800. It was $37,900 for 2025, and it moves each year with the Social Security cost-of-living percentage.
  • Income means money from every source except gifts or inheritances from a spouse, a lineal ancestor or a lineal descendant. If spouses live together, both incomes count.
  • The permanent residence is the dwelling plus its site, up to one acre, and related improvements. A single-family house, a unit in a multi-family complex and a manufactured home can all qualify.
  • A disabled applicant needs a certificate from a North Carolina licensed physician or from a governmental agency.
  • A married couple receives the full exclusion when only one spouse meets the age or disability test.

sections.h2: How is the disabled veteran exclusion different in North Carolina?
sections.html:
It excludes the first $45,000 of appraised value, and NCDOR's form states that there is no age or income limitation for it. The rule appears in G.S. 105-277.1C.

The veteran must be a North Carolina resident with an honorable or under-honorable-conditions separation, and must either receive benefits under 38 U.S.C. 2101 or hold VA certification of a service-connected, permanent and total disability. An unmarried surviving spouse can also claim it. Applicants complete Form NCDVA-9 with a Veterans Service Officer first, then file it with the county assessor.

sections.h2: What is the North Carolina circuit breaker deferral?
sections.html:
It caps the property tax bill as a share of income and defers the rest. Taxes are limited to 4.0% of income when income is at or under the eligibility limit, and to 5.0% when income is above the limit but within 150% of it.

For 2026, NCDOR prints those thresholds as $38,800 and $58,200. The owner must be 65 or totally and permanently disabled, live in North Carolina, and have owned and lived in the home as a permanent residence for at least five years. A new application is needed every year.

The deferred amount becomes a lien. Deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years fall due when something disqualifies the owner, such as a transfer, the owner's death or a move out of the home as a permanent residence.

sections.h2: How and when do you apply for North Carolina homestead relief?
sections.html:
File Form AV-9 with the county tax assessor during the listing period, which runs from the first business day of January through January 31. The assessor must still accept an application through June 1 before the tax year.

The form is the same for all three programs, so choose the one that fits your situation and ask the assessor if you meet the tests for more than one. Because the 2026 NCDOR form carries the 2026 figures, check the current year's form for new limits before you file, since the income limit changes annually.

sections.h2: What papers should a North Carolina applicant bring to the assessor?
sections.html:
Ask the assessor's office for its checklist, because counties handle the intake themselves. The statutes point to the evidence that most files need.

  • Proof of age, or the physician's or agency's certificate of total and permanent disability.
  • Income records for the prior year for the owner and for a spouse who lives in the home.
  • Proof that the property is the owner's permanent residence, including the acreage if the lot is larger than one acre.
  • For the circuit breaker, evidence of at least five years of ownership and occupancy.
  • For the veteran exclusion, the VA certification or the benefits record, plus the completed Form NCDVA-9.

Bringing the full set to the first visit saves a second trip, and it is the easiest way to stay inside the January 31 listing period.

sections.h2: How does the North Carolina income limit change from year to year?
sections.html:
NCDOR resets the figure annually using the Social Security cost-of-living percentage. The 2026 form prints $38,800, up from $37,900 for 2025, and the circuit breaker upper threshold of $58,200 equals 150% of the 2026 limit as the form prints it.

An owner who was just over the line one year can fall inside it the next, so a denial in one year does not settle later years. Check the figure for the tax year in question, and remember that the circuit breaker needs a fresh application every year while the other two programs may be renewed on a different schedule. Ask the assessor whether your county requires repeat filings.

sections.h2: What happens to this relief when you sell a North Carolina home?
sections.html:
A sale is a transfer, and a transfer is one of the events that makes deferred circuit breaker tax payable. Ask the county tax collector for a written payoff of any deferred amount before the closing date, so it can be settled at the table.

  • The seller pays the deed excise tax of $1.00 per $500, or fractional part, of the price to the register of deeds before recording.
  • Property tax is due each September 1, and interest of 2% begins on January 6 if the bill is unpaid.
  • An heir who inherits a home from a circuit breaker owner may face the deferred bill too, because the owner's death is one of the triggering events.

Deferred tax is a lien, so clear it with the tax collector rather than leaving it for the buyer to find. If you already receive any of the three benefits, tell the closing attorney or title company at the start, so the payoff request goes to the county early. Owners who inherit a home from someone who held the benefit should ask the same questions before listing.

faqs.q: What is the North Carolina homestead exclusion amount?
faqs.a: It is the greater of $25,000 or 50% of the home's appraised value for the elderly or disabled exclusion. The disabled veteran exclusion is a flat $45,000 of appraised value.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 income limit for the North Carolina exclusion?
faqs.a: The 2026 NCDOR form prints $38,800. The same form lists $37,900 as the 2025 limit.

faqs.q: Where do I file the North Carolina homestead application?
faqs.a: File Form AV-9 with your county tax assessor, not with the Department of Revenue. Veterans first complete Form NCDVA-9 with a Veterans Service Officer.

faqs.q: Can I get more than one North Carolina homestead program?
faqs.a: No. Each owner may receive the benefit of only one of the three programs.

faqs.q: What if I miss the January 31 filing date in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Your application can still be accepted. The assessor must take it through June 1 preceding the tax year.
